 Why Retirees Moving From California to Nevada Wait for the Nevada Driver’s License Before Converting to a Roth
 Vilma Rios Fri, November 13, 2026 at 3:12 AM MST 7 min read Quick Read 
 California taxes a Roth conversion until your residency ends, and the Franchise Tax Board decides that date from your full set of ties, not one document. 
 Converting after you move keeps the money outside California's tax base, yet it can still raise the rate on income earned before you left. 
 A Nevada driver's license is just one piece of residency evidence, but it marks a documented change of residence that supports your conversion timing.

 California to Nevada is one of the busiest retirement routes in the country. IRS migration data for 2022-2023 shows 26210 returns covering 43801 individuals moving from California to Nevada, which made Nevada California's third-largest destination by returns. For retirees with large traditional IRAs, the move opens a planning window. The 2025 State Tax Competitiveness Index places Nevada 7 on individual income tax and California 49. Whether California taxes a Roth conversion can depend on which side of the move it lands on. 
 RedTango/Shutterstock.com California Taxes Your Conversion Until Your Residency Ends 
 Federally, a converted amount goes into gross income for the year of the conversion (26 U.S.C. § 408A(d)(3)(A)(i)). IRS guidance says these amounts are "normally included in income on your return for the year that you converted them". California applies the same timing. For any part of the year you were a resident, California counts "all items of gross income and all deductions, regardless of source" under Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17041(i)(1)(A). The Franchise Tax Board (FTB) says part-year residents are taxed "on all income received while a resident and only on income from California sources while a nonresident," and that nonresidents are not taxed on pensions received after December 31, 1995. The FTB directs readers to FTB Pub. 1005 to see which retirement payments qualify.

 The hard part is pinning down the date your residence ends. The FTB will not give written opinions on residence because it is "a question of fact, not law." Under § 17014(c), a resident "continues to be a resident even though temporarily absent from the state." In one FTB example, declaring Nevada residence did not establish it because the taxpayer's closest connections were still in California. In another, a family that sold its California home, moved its belongings, enrolled the children in new schools and got a local driver's license became nonresidents on the day they moved. 
 What the Nevada License Proves 
 A Nevada driver's license is one piece of evidence in a facts-and-circumstances test. No federal or California rule requires it before you convert. Retirees use it as a checkpoint because it usually comes after the bigger ties have moved: the Nevada home, the sale or rental of the California house, and vehicle registration. Nevada's DMV tells new residents to get a license and register their vehicles soon after arriving. Converting after that point ties the conversion date to a documented change of legal residence, which helps if the FTB later asks when the move actually happened. 
 Same-Year Conversions Can Still Raise Your California Rate 
 California taxes part-year residents by applying an effective rate to their California taxable income. That rate is "the California tax on all income as if you were a California resident for the current tax year" divided by that income (§ 17041(b)(2)). So a conversion done after the move can stay outside California's tax base and still raise the rate on income you received before you left. 
 Example Household: The Garcias 
 The Garcias are a example married couple. They received $40,000 of income from January through June as California residents, move to Nevada on July 1 and plan a $100,000 conversion. 
 Convert in May, before the move: $40,000 + $100,000 = $140,000 of income in California's resident column. 
 Convert in October, after the license and home sale: Only the $40,000 is California-taxed. The rate on it is figured using all $140,000 as if they had been residents all year, which drives that rate up. 
 Convert the following January: They are Nevada residents for the whole conversion year, so California's part-year rules don't apply to that year. 
 In all three cases, the $100,000 counts as federal gross income in the year of the conversion. 
 Federal Rules That Follow You to Nevada 
 RMDs come first. You "can't convert amounts that must be distributed" for a given year. The RMD starting age is 73 for people born from 1951 through 1959 and 75 for people born in 1960 or later. 
 No undo. Recharacterization is not available for conversions (§ 408A(d)(6)(B)(iii)). 
 Pro-rata rule. For figuring tax on distributions, "all individual retirement plans shall be treated as 1 contract" under § 408(d)(2). Conversions are reported on Form 8606, and Treasury Regulation 1.408A-4 sets out the conversion requirements (26 CFR 1.408A-4). 
 Medicare surcharges. The base Part B premium for 2026 is $202.90 per month. Joint filers with income above $218,000 pay at least $81.20 an extra per month, and the threshold for single filers is $109,000. Medicare sets premiums from income two years earlier, so a conversion done in 2026 affects 2028 premiums. Leaving California does nothing to reduce the income that sets these surcharges. 
 Who Should Skip the Post-Move Conversion 
 A conversion after the move works best for retirees who have fully relocated, can pay the federal tax from savings outside the IRA, and expect their tax rate on withdrawals to stay the same or rise. It fits these households less well: 
 Retirees who keep a California home or spend long periods there, since the FTB may still treat them as residents. 
 Anyone who would pay the conversion tax from IRA money, which shrinks the amount that ends up in the Roth. 
 Households whose income falls just under a Medicare surcharge threshold. 
 Retirees who expect to be in a lower bracket later or who plan to give their IRA to charity. 
 If you need to report income, IRS guidance warns that you "may have to increase your withholding or make estimated tax payments." 
 What to Check Before Scheduling the Conversion 
 Write down your departure date and keep records of each tie you cut. Then decide whether converting the following January is worth the wait to stay clear of California's effective-rate calculation for the move year. Before setting a conversion amount, check your RMD age and where your income falls relative to the 2026 Medicare thresholds two years out. A 2026 conversion sets your 2028 premiums. Your license date can support your residence case, but the FTB looks at your full set of ties to decide when you stopped being a California resident. (The low-tax years after retiring and before RMDs are often the cheapest time to convert at all, something we sized up in a free Roth Window guide.)
